entry.title: What I Learned (and Wish I'd Done Differently) at TechCabal's Moonshot
entry.content:
Why I Was There

A few months ago, I moved from Port Harcourt to Lagos with one mission: to tap into the city's tech ecosystem by attending events, meeting top talent, and getting the kind of exposure that could change my life.

Then, honestly, not much happened. My first months in Lagos were quiet. No events, no big introductions, just me, a laptop, and a plan that hadn't started yet.

That changed with TechCabal's Moonshot, my first tech event since the move. I loved it, but I also left with a list of things I wish I had done differently. This post covers both.

Arrival

I was so excited that I got to the National Theatre at about 8:30am, an hour and a half before the 10am start. It didn't matter. The place was already swarming with people, and from the energy around me, they were just as excited as I was.

Getting in was painless. I scanned my ticket, collected my tag, and walked in. No queues!

The hard part came after. From the start, I found the central hall confusing to navigate, and I spent my first stretch of the day just trying to work out where everything was.

The Sessions

The sessions are where Moonshot's tech focus really showed. This year's theme was "Courage & Conviction: Building for a New World," and three threads ran through the day for me: AI, the future of money, and building companies that last.

With talks running on several stages at once, I couldn't be everywhere, so I followed the topics closest to what I care about.

  • The State of AI in Nigeria: A panel on where Nigeria actually stands with AI, moderated by Dr. Olubayo Adekanmbi on the Big Tech and Enterprise Stage. It made me see AI as a data and infrastructure problem as much as a model problem. Without good local data, reliable compute, and trained people, the technology stays a demo. As someone with a data engineering background, that was the part of the stack I felt closest to.
  • Stablecoins & Monetary Sovereignty: Seun Lanlege's talk on the Future of Money Stage asked how stablecoins fit into a country's control over its own money. It changed how I think about payment rails. The technology can move value in seconds, but the harder questions are trust, regulation, and who gets to set the rules.
  • Forty Years A Tech Bro: What It Takes To Build Something That Lasts: Sir Demola Aladekomo, in conversation with Fu'ad Lawal, spoke about building across decades instead of funding cycles. It was a useful counterweight to the speed-obsessed side of tech: lasting companies are built on patience and fundamentals more than hype.
  • Building Africa's Workforce for the Global Economy: Joel Ogunsola's talk on the Workshop Stage was about preparing African talent to compete globally. It spoke directly to why I moved to Lagos. Opportunity tends to find people who put themselves in the room, and skills count for more when the right people can see them.

Hearing these ideas in one place made the ecosystem feel far more real than reading about it online ever had.

Walking the Exhibition Floor

If the sessions gave me ideas, the exhibition tour gave me exposure. Every company had a booth with banners, merchandise, and someone ready to explain what made their product different.

My favorite stop was Cloudflare. I'd been wondering whether they plan to support VPS-style machine provisioning for people who deploy on their cloud, so I asked. The answer was no. It wasn't what I'd hoped for, but getting a straight answer from the people who would know was worth the walk.

I also spoke with Liners, a software company that offers reviews and SEO boosting for African software products, and with a sales representative from Rexx, which describes itself as Africa's first AI-native banking solution. Other booths on my route included Grey, a fintech platform for cross-border payments, GoPaddi, an AI-powered platform for travel, tourism, hospitality, and business management, and Zikoko, a Nigerian digital and entertainment platform.

The People

Networking was the reason I moved, so I made a point of talking to people from different corners of tech. These are some of the new friends I made:

  • ID Inyang is a software engineer who builds practical applications for real-world problems. He specializes in backend development and system design, with a focus on software that is scalable, reliable, and efficient. Backend and system design is where I want to go deeper, so he's someone I plan to keep learning from.
  • Brian Ibekwe is a product manager at ReadPulse, where he works on building, improving, and growing the platform. Talking to someone who thinks in terms of users and growth gave me a useful contrast to my own more technical view of products.
  • Emmanuel Obiabo works mostly with TypeScript and Rust, contributes to open source, and writes about whatever catches his interest. Much of his open-source work has been on blockchain projects in the Stellar ecosystem, and he is a long-time Linux user. You can read more about him here. His path through open source is one I'm curious to follow.
  • Marilyn is a UI/UX designer. Her portfolio includes TideReader, an AI-powered adaptive reading platform, Delve, a gamified language-learning platform, and Bubblr, a safe social media app for kids. Her case studies are a reminder that products live or die on design, and I'd love to work on something where engineering and design are in the same room.
  • Mauteen is a product design engineer who works where design meets engineering. That overlap is exactly what I want to understand better, so I'm glad we connected.
  • Eric is a creative software developer who builds mobile apps, backend systems, and web platforms end to end. He's a fellow builder, and the kind of person I'd happily build with.
  • Mary Adejumo: A product manager at Rex Microfinance Bank, where she owns the mobile app and website of the digital bank. She also built FindRyd, an AI-powered navigation app that gives delivery riders directions in landmarks instead of metres, taking it from 85 rider interviews to a tested prototype. A member of the Best Product Discovery Team in the 2026 PLA APM Fellowship, she writes things down until a team can build from them and tests the riskiest assumption first, which is a habit I want to pick up.

What I Wish I Had Done Differently

I'd call these small preparations, not big mistakes. But each one would have made the day easier.

1. Carry a personal card

Over and over, I did the same thing: pulled out my phone, found someone's LinkedIn or X handle, and typed mine in return. It was slow, it interrupted the conversation, and it only worked if both of us had the patience for it.

A personal card would have turned that into a two-second exchange. It doesn't have to be fancy: my name, what I do, and a QR code to my LinkedIn or GitHub. It would also give people something to remember me by when they leave a crowded venue with a bag of merchandise and a head full of names.

2. Wear something that starts conversations

Moonshot was a sea of similar tags and similar outfits, and it was hard to stand out. Branded wear, like a shirt or hoodie with my name, my role, or something I'm building, would have done some of the introducing for me. People would have had a reason to ask about it, and I wouldn't have had to open every conversation cold. It would also have made me easier to find again after a first meeting.

3. Plan my route through the day

I arrived early and still got lost in the halls. With sessions running on several stages at once, it's easy to drift toward whatever is closest instead of what matters. Next time, I'll bookmark my sessions the night before, note which stage each one is on, and leave gaps for the exhibition floor, so I'm choosing my time instead of just reacting to the crowd.

Final Thoughts

I moved to Lagos for moments like this one. Moonshot gave me sessions that sharpened my thinking, a floor full of companies to talk to, and a handful of people I'm glad to know. Next time, I'll show up with a card, an outfit that speaks for me, and a plan for the day. If you were at Moonshot, I'd love to hear what you'd do differently. And if this post was useful, share it with someone heading to their first tech event.

entry.title: Learning Technical Skills in the Age of SI
entry.content:
Introduction

Like many technical or skilled persons in the world at the moment, in the age of SI[1] it's becoming increasingly hard to feel special about the technical skill you possess, especially a skill like software mastery or software engineering. In recent times, I have had to come face to face with the reality that what made me special (with the hands in the air, defensively), in terms of my technical skills and experience in software programming, is largely not special anymore.

Now I have a real issue: Why should I invest real time like was done in the past, to gain mastery of topics that now feels very ephemeral? Why should I commit my weekend to understanding how Python's dictionary actually works under the hood and care about the details linked to open addressing, when I can generate more features far beyond my control in a product others could just as well vibe code?

At my most recent workplace (sad memories of my employed self), apart from the issues linked with lack of a concrete vision for the company's moat, I basically clocked out at some point, and just became a feature sprouting organism, attending demo after demo to wow always almost-at-the-verge-of-paying-clients. This was sad for me, because outside making a living with the skills I had acquired, I do genuinely love solving problems with the tools in my arsenal that actually ended up being used by people.

What was it really about for you?

The answer to this question would probably justify most people's stance on whether to bother committing to learning certain technical skills, if it was solely about implementing a feature, I guess you're better off moving fast and generating one with an LLM or some agent of sorts, but if it was really about mastering systems, understanding principles and unconsciously or consciously transferring those skills to other unrelated domains then the fear of being replaced should be less (notice how I said less, it doesn't go away). This does not invalidate the fear of losing out on a race of doing so much more with limited time and capital compared to any other time in history.

My Personal initial motivation

For me, it was always about mastery, I mean that mastery made my work easier, but I always loved the bits and bytes of it all, the quirks you had to get used to, and understand why they were, the rationales, the processes, it made committing to mastery very rewarding. All these contributed to building one's problem solving muscles across domains. For example I do this thing in my real life activities, where I try to do a lot of things concurrently in a beautifully scheduled way, mimicking asynchronous programming style: Like how I try to hack my chores and wait times on other activity by using those wait times to attend to other pending activities and I do it consciously and get excitement from being my own asynchronous runtime.

Is History Repeating itself?

I am sure a certain set of skilled person experienced things like this in the past, take for example, In the chess world, computers have practically perfected playing chess, and have since surpassed humans, but people still study it, and deep understanding separates good players from great ones. And that mastery is not any less valuable because it's beneath a computer's.

I think the same argument can be made for what is happening to software engineering and maths at this point in history, of course everyone can spin up a React App and get a well documented API powering it, but I believe it's a matter of time, before the mass hysteria dies off (this is actual wishful thinking) and people get bored of the AI hype. Is there a place of SI in work? of course, but I have accepted that mastery is personal and it does in fact reward more even outside of the specific domain of application.

Conclusion

I could be terribly wrong, man! I don't know the future, but this sounds quite reasonable, so if you're reading this from some distant day in the future and you laugh at my sheer misdirection on how things were going to go, I want you to know I too was open to the possibility that things happened in ways I could not have predicted. Soooo!! Do whatever makes you happy, and if that includes mastery of the internals of Fortran or memorizing factorials of a very large number, by all means go crazy. I am actively looking for a new role as a Software Engineer at the moment. Here is my CV

  1. SI: Super Intelligence - President Donald Trump signed an Executive Order on September 29, 2026, officially directing federal agencies to replace the terms "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) and "AI" with "Super Intelligence" (SI) in all official correspondence, public communications, and non-statutory documents. Read more ↩

entry.title: Mastering the Crate and Module System in the Rust
entry.content:
Introduction

Once your program or project starts to grow, the need to introduce more files and organize your project's structure becomes crucial to maintaining sanity and ensuring a productive coding environment. Rust offers the concepts of crates and modules, and mastering these can help you shape your next project in a systematic way that enhances understanding and contributions to larger Rust projects. This piece will dive into the intricacies of the crate and module system, providing clarity on their roles, differences, and the best practices around them.

Packages are not Crates, and Vice Versa

This has often been the stumbling block for many developers new to Rust. Common materials assert that crates are the building blocks of Rust projects and, by extension, the smallest unit of compilation. This leads to the misconception that when a new project is created, that project is, in itself, a crate. However, this is not true.

Creating a New Project

When you start a new project using Cargo with the command:

$ cargo new rust-projects

The output indicates that a binary application package has been created:

Created binary (application) `rust-projects` package

This initializes your project directory and generates several files. The hierarchical structure of the generated files appears as follows:

$ ls rust-projects
Cargo.toml
src

$ ls rust-projects/src
main.rs

Every package contains a Cargo.toml file and a src directory with a main.rs file (in the binary case), but the package itself is not the crate. It is technically correct to refer to a package in Rust as a folder containing a Cargo.toml file — you can make a regular directory a package by adding a valid Cargo.toml file.

Crates Explained

When a package is created, Rust automatically generates a binary crate rooted at src/main.rs. If you wish to create a library crate, you can use:

$ cargo new --lib <lib-package-name>

This generates a standard Cargo package, but houses a lib.rs file instead of main.rs. The distinction between files like main.rs and lib.rs is crucial, as it indicates whether a package is a binary or a library.

Key Definitions

  • Package: A housing unit for crates. A package contains at least one crate rooted at src/main.rs or src/lib.rs.
  • Crate: The compiled piece of code, which can either be a binary or a library. Each package allows for multiple binary crates (and can also include dependencies).

By defining packages and crates in this way, it becomes easier to grasp syntax such as crate::<path>. This directly translates to the <path> item located in the src/main.rs file, which is the crate root for binary packages, and src/lib.rs for library packages.

Modules: The Organizational Structure

While packages help you group crates at a project level, modules provide a structured organization for different features or parts of your code. Think of your package as a house filled with various items sourced from various brands — some you create and others you buy. It's your responsibility to organize these items in a way that makes sense for your desired house setting.

The Importance of Modules

Consider a house where all items are crammed together. This leads to confusion and makes it difficult to find the necessary items. The clearer the organization within your project or code, the more efficient you can be. This concept of organization is the primary benefit modules provide — not just in Rust, but in every programming language.

Basic Usage of Modules

To define a module in Rust, the mod keyword is utilized. For instance:

// src/main.rs

mod kitchen {
    struct Cooker(String);
    struct Heater(String);
    struct Table;
}

fn main() {
    println!("Hello World!");
}

Here, a module named kitchen is created, containing three structs: Cooker, Heater, and Table. To utilize an item from this module, the path to the item must be specified at the point where the item is needed.

Path to Items Inside Modules

If you need to access an item from this module:

// inside the main function
let cooker = kitchen::Cooker("Pressure Cooker".to_string());

This statement effectively directs Rust to navigate to the kitchen module to access the Cooker item.

Visibility in Modules

Items within modules are private by default, which means they are not accessible from outside unless designated as public using the pub keyword. For example:

mod kitchen {
    pub struct Cooker(String); // the String item inside the Cooker is private
    pub struct Heater(String); // so is the String item inside the Heater

    struct Table; // Still private
}

Even if Cooker is public, its contents remain private unless stated explicitly. This ensures encapsulation and keeps the module organized and maintainable.

Large Codebase Management in Rust

For projects evolving into larger codebases, managing dependencies and organization becomes critical. This section covers best practices for structuring large Rust projects.

Dependency Management

Cargo.toml: This central configuration file plays a crucial role in managing dependencies. You must specify the dependencies your crate is using here, enabling straightforward integration and updates. By allowing version control directly within this file, Rust ensures compatibility with the modules or packages you rely on.

[dependencies]
rand = "0.8"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

Using external crates: You can include external libraries available from crates.io, effectively reducing development time and enhancing functional capabilities.

# Adding an external crate
[dependencies]
log = "0.4"

Your project can then use external libraries seamlessly in your codebase, allowing for rich functionality with little overhead.

Module Organization Strategies

Logical grouping: Organizing functionality into logically cohesive modules reduces complexity. For instance, if you have functionality related to user management, implement that in a user.rs module, while maintaining a separate product.rs for product-related functionality. This keeps separation of concerns clear.

Namespacing: The use of prefixes in module names can help maintain clarity, especially when dealing with numerous modules. By structuring your modules distinctly, you can easily avoid naming collisions that would lead to conflicts at compile time.

Advanced Module Usage

Modules in Rust offer a breadth of functionality that can enhance code clarity and reusability. This section dives into advanced techniques for modules.

Nested Modules

Nested modules allow you to create more complex hierarchical structures, which can help in organizing similar functionality together. Here's an example of how to define nested modules:

mod server {
    pub mod routes {
        pub fn get_user() {
            println!("Getting user");
        }
    }

    pub mod handlers {
        pub fn handle_request() {
            println!("Handling request");
        }
    }
}

To access these nested modules, the syntax becomes a bit more complex. You need to specify the full path:

fn main() {
    server::routes::get_user();
    server::handlers::handle_request();
}

This organization not only keeps your project tidy but also clearly delineates functionality, making it easier for others to understand the codebase.

Public Interfaces and Privacy

Understanding visibility is crucial for maintaining a clean boundary between different parts of your code. Any item marked as pub can be accessed from the outside, while those without this modifier are private. Here's how to correctly declare visibility:

mod kitchen {
    pub struct Cooker(pub String); // Both the struct and its field are public.
    pub struct Heater(String); // Struct is public, but field remains private.

    impl Heater {
        // This method can be public if needed
        pub fn new(name: String) -> Heater {
            Heater(name)
        }
    }
}

This approach allows for a flexible API while maintaining internal encapsulation where necessary.

Performance Optimization with Modules

Understanding how to structure your modules and leverage Rust's compilation process can lead to optimized performance.

Optimizing for Compilation

When you split your code into smaller modules, Rust's incremental compilation can speed up the build process. When only one module is changed, only that particular module needs to be recompiled instead of the entire project. This can be a significant advantage in large applications.

Memory Usage

Using modules wisely can allow Rust to optimize memory usage at runtime. By compartmentalizing functionality, unnecessary data can often be discarded if it's only used within a particular context:

#[inline(always)]
fn expensive_function() -> Result<String, String> {
    // Hypothetical expensive operation
    Ok("Result".to_string())
}

By marking functions inline, you can reduce the overhead of function calls and streamline performance in high-frequency usage scenarios.

Working with Crates: Dependency Management and Structuring

Understanding how to manage and structure crates within Rust applications is key to building robust applications.

Cargo.toml: The Heartbeat of Dependency Management

The Cargo.toml file is crucial for managing dependencies and specifying package metadata. Here is how you can structure it:

[package]
name = "my_project"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2018"

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
chrono = "0.4"

By keeping dependencies well-organized and up to date, you ensure your project remains stable and compatible with other libraries.

Case Study: Real-world Application Structure

Consider a Rust web application structured for a blog. The project can be divided into several parts: a main entry point for the server, one for handling database interactions, one for authentication, and another for utility functions.

my_blog/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── main.rs   # Main entry point.
    ├── db.rs     # Database interactions.
    ├── auth.rs   # Authentication logic.
    └── utils.rs  # Utility functions.

Each module can be further divided upon reaching significant complexity, forming yet another layer of hierarchy.

Practical Examples and Use Cases

To solidify understanding, let's run through practical examples that demonstrate these concepts in action.

1. Basic Module Usage

Imagine a library to handle mathematical operations:

// src/math.rs

pub mod operations {
    pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
        a + b
    }

    pub fn multiply(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
        a * b
    }
}

You can call it directly within your main program:

// src/main.rs

mod math;

fn main() {
    let sum = math::operations::add(5, 7);
    let product = math::operations::multiply(5, 7);
    println!("Sum: {}, Product: {}", sum, product);
}

2. Using External Crates

Let's include the popular serde crate for serialization and deserialization. Here's how to use it:

# Cargo.toml

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"
// src/user.rs

use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct User {
    pub username: String,
    pub email: String,
}
// src/main.rs

mod user;

use user::User;

fn main() {
    let user = User {
        username: String::from("john_doe"),
        email: String::from("john.doe@example.com"),
    };

    let serialized_user = serde_json::to_string(&user).unwrap();
    println!("Serialized User: {}", serialized_user);
}

In this example, we're leveraging an external crate to efficiently handle data in our application.

Conclusion

Mastering the crate and module system in Rust is essential for building maintainable, scalable applications. Understanding the differences between packages and crates, along with the organizational capabilities offered by modules, allows you to create more efficient and effective codebases. By adopting the best practices highlighted throughout this article, you can elevate your programming skills and foster clean code structures that accommodate growth and complexity. Embrace these tools and watch your Rust projects flourish, ready to tackle broader functionality and larger codebases.

Technical Verdict

In conclusion, a profound understanding of crates and modules not only enhances your capability to write efficient Rust code but also empowers you to navigate complex projects confidently. With careful management of packages, robust dependency handling, and organized module structures, Rust developers can cultivate a prolific development environment conducive to both individual and collaborative growth.

By continuously expanding your knowledge and adapting your practices to leverage the power of crates and modules, you prepare yourself to create the next generation of Rust applications efficiently.

entry.title: 6 Python Tips That Quietly Level Up Your Code
entry.content:
Introduction

If you're like me at the moment, you've gotten to a point in your software development journey where you find yourself writing code to tick off tasks from a task board or complete features for a sprint. At such times, the focus sometimes shifts from poetic code to functional code (not implying that functional code cannot be easily poetic, but it takes mastery and experience to maintain such quality when working under tight deadlines). It is at this point that you're more concerned with getting things to work than with how they feel and look.

Below are some Python tips and tricks I use and believe are not as emphasized as they should be. They would do good to your mental health when writing code and, more importantly, when updating that code 3 months from now.

TL;DR:

  1. Inline single-line blocks in block expressions
  2. Use underscores to delimit a large number
  3. Dictionary comprehension
  4. Using the setdefault dictionary method
  5. Ignore exceptions with contextlib.suppress
  6. Multiple statements on a single line

1. Inline single-line blocks in block expressions

some_condition = True

if some_condition:
    print("Some Condition is True")
else:
    print("Some Condition is Falsey")

In the code sample above, the correct conventional 4-space indentation is used for the expression in a block expression. But in this particular case, the block contains just a single expression. This might be a trivial case, but many such scenarios arise a lot in functional codebases, and you can save some real estate by inlining the single expression on the same line as the if block.

some_condition = True

if some_condition: print("Some Condition is True")
else: print("Some Condition is False")

This is perfectly valid Python, and in some cases makes your code easier to read and follow. Do note that you can only inline single-line expressions; if the expression is multi-line, you have to use the conventional 4-space indentation to communicate the block scope to the Python interpreter. If, however, always using the block format for block expressions works better for you, by all means do use that way.

2. Use underscores to delimit a large number

This is more common than some of the tips on this list. Still, for the uninitiated, here goes nothing. When dealing with literal values in your application, it can be counterintuitive or even error-prone having to figure out the value of a large literal number at a glance, and this could very well mean the only thing standing between you and your continued state of mental flow. Python — and some other high-level programming languages like Rust — allows the use of _ in literal numbers to show their unit.

obscure_large_number = 3422345365
clear_large_number = 3_422_345_365  # it is easier to tell the unit value when delimited by underscores

3. Dictionary comprehension

The more popular sibling of the comprehension family in Python is the list comprehension, where a list is generated from an iterable in a single expression without needing a conventional for-loop to populate the list. This same process can be used to generate a dictionary or a set.

Let's imagine we have a list of names and want to generate a dictionary whose key is a name and whose value is the length of that name's characters. We can achieve this with a traditional for-loop, like so:

names = ["Brian", "Anthony", "Maryann", "Joseph", "Emediong"]
word_count = {}
for name in names:
    word_count[name] = len(name)

print(word_count)

# Output
# {'Brian': 5, 'Anthony': 7, 'Maryann': 7, 'Joseph': 6, 'Emediong': 8}

Now this same functionality can be achieved through dictionary comprehension in a more comprehensive way (pun intended). It looks just like a list comprehension, but curly braces are used, and a colon separates the key from the value being derived from the iterable.

names = ["Brian", "Anthony", "Maryann", "Joseph", "Emediong"]
word_count = {name: len(name) for name in names}

# general dictionary comprehension syntax
# {key: derived_value for key in sequence}

print(word_count)

# Output
# {'Brian': 5, 'Anthony': 7, 'Maryann': 7, 'Joseph': 6, 'Emediong': 8}

4. Using the setdefault dictionary method

Still on the topic of working with dictionaries in Python: there are times you wish to update a value in a dictionary, but you have to ensure that said key already exists in the dictionary, or Python would raise a KeyError. You could write a one-liner to check for the existence of the key before updating the key's value, like so:

race_laps = {"Brian": 234, "Anthony": 525, "Maryann": 534, "Joseph": 467, "Emediong": 876}


new_lap_data = {
    "Brian": 34,
    "Anthony": 45,
    "Felix": 100,
}

for driver, distance in new_lap_data.items():
    if driver in race_laps:
        race_laps[driver] += distance
    else:
        race_laps[driver] = distance

But it is clear that this introduces unnecessary verbosity into our program by introducing an if/else block. We can use the setdefault method of a dictionary to set a default value for a key before trying to update it, in case it is not present in the dictionary. The same logic above can be rewritten like so with the setdefault method:

race_laps = {"Brian": 234, "Anthony": 525, "Maryann": 534, "Joseph": 467, "Emediong": 876}

new_lap_data = {
    "Brian": 34,
    "Anthony": 45,
    "Felix": 100,
}

for driver, distance in new_lap_data.items():
    race_laps.setdefault(driver, 0)  # this sets a value of 0 for the driver if not already in the dictionary
    race_laps[driver] += distance

This approach makes the code more concise and is more Pythonic than the structure with the if/else block.

5. Ignore exceptions with contextlib.suppress

Sometimes we want to catch an exception and then do nothing with it — we're catching it to prevent the program from breaking or stopping, and to continue with the flow. This can be done with a try/except block, and if you have no logic to run in the except block, you can use the pass statement to indicate nothingness.

def do_some_action():
    # some action that might fail but is not critical to the whole program
    pass

while True:
    try:
        do_some_action()
    except Exception:
        pass

In the code sample above, we put the logic that might raise an exception in the try block and then ignore the cases where it raises. This structure forces us to use a block; we could apply the first tip from this post to further improve the structure and gain some real estate.

def do_some_action():
    # some action that might fail but is not critical to the whole program
    pass

while True:
    try: do_some_action()
    except Exception: pass

However, we can go even further and use a standard library class that is not very well known, to suppress exceptions and continue with your program as if they hadn't happened. The contextlib standard library provides a class called suppress that can be used to suppress exceptions in our code. Going back to the same example as above, the code can be rewritten with suppress as follows:

from contextlib import suppress


def do_some_action():
    # some action that might fail but is not critical to the whole program
    pass

while True:
    with suppress(Exception):  # the exception is suppressed silently
        do_some_action()

This suppresses the exception type passed to it, and just like the normal exception rule, a parent class can suppress child exception classes. You can also suppress multiple exceptions with a with block by passing more exception classes to suppress, separated by commas.

with suppress(ValueError, ValidationError):  # ValueError and ValidationError are suppressed here
    ...

6. Multiple statements on a single line

Conventionally, a newline in Python code declares the end of a statement and the start of another. Some other programming languages use semicolons to separate statements, but Python is a whitespace language. Regardless, semicolons can be used in Python, and in rare situations you might need to put more than one statement on a single line — you can do this by terminating each statement with a semicolon.

# Conventional Python statement flow
# each newline denotes a different statement
a = 1
b = 2
print(f"A = {a}")
print(f"B = {b}")

# using semicolons to separate statements
a = 1;  # this is also valid Python
b = 3;
print(f"A = {a}");

# putting multiple statements on a single line
a = 10;print(f"A = {a}")

Clearly, putting each statement on its own line leads to better readability for your code, but in rare scenarios, knowing that multiple statements can be placed on a single line can give you the ability to do certain magic.

Conclusion

I love reading and learning about these little neat tricks and try to apply them when I see fit in my projects. If there are similar tricks you know and would love to share, I'd love to hear them.

entry.title: My FastAPI Project Blueprint
entry.content:
I've refined this structure in production environments serving over 500+ concurrent users; it scales effortlessly, stays sane to maintain, and keeps productivity at full throttle.

TL;DR

If you just want to use the template FastAPI structure directly in your project, check out this GitHub repo for the complete project structure.

Introduction

I have worked with FastAPI almost daily in the last year. During that period, I developed a standard project structure that works exceptionally well to keep me motivated to make changes and add features easily, and it also scales incredibly.

In this post, I will break down every part of my FastAPI go-to architecture — the one I optimize whenever I'm starting a new project or refactoring an old one. Whether you're trying to ship ideas faster, organize your growing codebase, or harden your app's security, this structure will help you build confidently and evolve your project like a pro.

Project Structure

.
├── Makefile
├── logs/
│   └── app.log
└── app/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── api_router.py
    ├── dependencies.py
    ├── logger.py
    ├── main.py
    ├── middlewares.py
    ├── settings.py
    ├── routers/
    │   ├── admin.py
    │   ├── auth.py
    │   └── products.py
    ├── schemas/
    │   ├── admin.py
    │   ├── auth.py
    │   └── products.py
    └── services/
        ├── admin.py
        ├── auth.py
        └── products.py

The App Directory

The app directory is the engine and core of the application. It contains all the modules and code needed to power the majority of use cases for a backend infrastructure. I'll explain each directory and module in the app directory and justify their use, pointing out common issues and highlighting steps taken to improve code quality and developer experience.

__init__.py

It is standard practice to include an __init__.py file in every Python package; this helps to declare a folder as a regular Python package.

api_router.py

I use this as a central module for managing all my routers in my application. This enables me to have features like version controlling with /v1/users, /v2/users while keeping the codebase easy to follow and clean.

# app/api_router.py

from fastapi import APIRouter

api_v1 = APIRouter(prefix="/v1")
api_v2 = APIRouter(prefix="/v2")

# include routes to a root route
# from app.routers import routers as user_routers
# api_v1.include_router(users_routers)

logger.py

Logging is a crucial part of every software application. It gives visibility into the operation of any running software application and can help guide resolution of issues and bugs when they do happen — and they will happen.

Instead of getting overwhelmed with configurations, this template works for me in almost all my projects. You can extend it by setting up an external handler to connect your log records to a pretty dashboard or analytics tool. This particular configuration allows me to group logs by day, achieved with the TimedRotatingFileHandler, making the process of debugging much easier.

# app/logger.py

import logging
import json

from logging.handlers import TimedRotatingFileHandler

logger = logging.getLogger()


class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record):
        log_record = {
            "timestamp": self.formatTime(record, self.datefmt),
            "level": record.levelname,
            "module": record.module,
            "funcName": record.funcName,
            "lineno": record.lineno,
            "message": record.getMessage(),
        }
        return json.dumps(log_record)


file_handler = TimedRotatingFileHandler(
    "logs/app.log", when="midnight", interval=1 / 86400, backupCount=7
)

file_handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())

logger.handlers = [file_handler]
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

main.py

The main module is the entry point into the application. Most of the security policies and rules for the application are set up here.

# app/main.py

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from datetime import datetime, UTC
from fastapi import FastAPI

from starlette.middleware.trustedhost import TrustedHostMiddleware
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
from fastapi.middleware.gzip import GZipMiddleware
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from fastapi.requests import Request
from fastapi import HTTPException
from fastapi import FastAPI

from slowapi import Limiter
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address

from redis import asyncio as aioredis

from app.logger import logger
from app.api_router import api
from app.settings import Settings
from app.middlewares import log_request_middleware

settings = Settings()


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    yield


def initiate_app():
    app = FastAPI(
        title="FastAPI Sample Project",
        summary="API for FastAPI Sample Project",
        lifespan=lifespan,
    )

    origins = [
        # Add allowed origins here
    ]

    app.add_middleware(
        CORSMiddleware,
        allow_origins=origins,
        allow_credentials=True,
        allow_methods=["*"],
        allow_headers=["*"],
    )

    # tweak this to see the most efficient size
    app.add_middleware(GZipMiddleware, minimum_size=100)
    app.add_middleware(
        TrustedHostMiddleware,
        allowed_hosts=[
            # Add allowed hosts here, this controls host that the application can be hosted on
        ],
    )
    app.add_middleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware, dispatch=log_request_middleware)

    # this handles rate limiting protecting the API from abuse or Denial of Service Attacks
    limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)
    app.state.limiter = limiter

    app.include_router(api)
    return app


app = initiate_app()


@app.exception_handler(HTTPException)
async def http_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: HTTPException):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=exc.status_code,
        content={
            "detail": exc.detail,
            "path": request.url.path,
            "timestamp": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(),
        },
    )


@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def global_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: Exception):
    logger.error(f"Unexpected error: {str(exc)}")

    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=500,
        content={
            "detail": "An unexpected error occurred",
            "path": request.url.path,
        },
    )


@app.get("/", tags=["Root"])
async def root():
    # this redirects root requests to the docs page
    return RedirectResponse("/docs")

settings.py

I have discovered that using Pydantic's BaseSettings model makes handling of environment variables easy and clean. Types can be defined for the environment variables and they are validated at app startup time, and default values can be provided for optional environment variables.

# app/settings.py

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
from pydantic import ConfigDict, AnyUrl


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = ConfigDict(env_file=".env")

    example_secret: str = "example secret value"

    JWT_SECRET: str  # required environment variable
    JWT_ALGORITHM: str = "HS256"  # optional environment variable with default value

dependencies.py

I use this module to group my custom route dependencies. Common dependencies like get_db, which is commonly used to get a session to interact with the database, can be declared here. Using a dedicated module for dependencies makes code organization better and more modular, since usually different routes depend on these dependencies. Testing is also easier since logic can be tested in isolation.

middlewares.py

I use this module to group all the custom middlewares I define for my application. The modular benefits outlined for a dedicated dependencies module also apply here.

Directories

Routers

I find that creating a module for each logical grouping of routes makes development lovely and easier — for example, an auth.py module for all routes relating to user authentication and profile management, a products.py module for all routes relating to product management, and admin.py for all routes related to the admin API.

I try to keep my route functions to at most 2 lines of code. The route function simply lays out the route and defines the dependencies and query parameters needed, while the logic for each route function is defined in a service function.

# app/routers/auth.py

from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import EmailStr
from fastapi.routing import APIRouter
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from fastapi import Depends, Body, BackgroundTasks

from app.dependencies import get_db
from app.schemas import auth as auth_schemas
from app.services import auth as auth_services

router = APIRouter(prefix="/auth", tags=["Authentication"])


EmailBody = Annotated[EmailStr, Body(embed=True)]
DBDep = Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(get_db)]


@router.post("/signup", response_model=auth_schemas.UserModel)
async def signup(
    db: DBDep,
    bg_task: BackgroundTasks,
    request_data: auth_schemas.UserSignUpData,
):
    return await auth_services.signup_user(request_data, db, bg_task)

The route function is easy on the eyes: the business logic is handled in the service function, while the route focuses on defining the dependencies and requirements in the form of a JSON body or query parameters.

Schemas

All my Pydantic models go into the schema module. Just like the routers directory, the schemas directory houses all the schema modules. Usually I match each route module with a corresponding schema module and a service module — this way each component of my application is grouped in a very logical and predictable way. An example of a schema module is auth.py, shown below.

# app/schemas/auth.py

from uuid import UUID
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field


class UserSignUpData(BaseModel):
    password: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=8)]
    email: Annotated[EmailStr, Field(max_length=254)]


class UserModel(BaseModel):
    id: UUID

    email: EmailStr
    date_created: datetime
    date_updated: datetime

Services

The services directory houses modules with the actual business logic to process the backend functionality. This can include API calls to third-party services, functions to make query calls to the database, and so on. Separating them this way allows a major separation of concerns between the route's API requirements and the actual implementation.

And just like I do for the routers and schemas directories, I match each module in those directories with a corresponding module for the component covered in the services directory. Working with the running example for the auth component:

# app/services/auth.py

from datetime import timedelta

from fastapi import HTTPException
from passlib.context import CryptContext
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.settings import Settings
from app.models import User as UserDB
from app.schemas import auth as auth_schema

settings = Settings()

JWT_SECRET = settings.JWT_SECRET
JWT_ALGORITHM = settings.JWT_ALGORITHM

ACCESS_TOKEN_LIFESPAN = timedelta(days=2)
REFRESH_TOKEN_LIFESPAN = timedelta(days=5)

pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")
oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="v1/auth/token")


def verify_password(plain_password: str, hashed_password: str):
    return pwd_context.verify(plain_password, hashed_password)


def get_password_hash(password: str):
    return pwd_context.hash(password)


async def get_user(email: str, session: AsyncSession) -> UserDB | None:
    stmt = select(UserDB).where(UserDB.email == email)
    result = await session.execute(stmt)
    return result.scalar_one_or_none()


async def create_user(
    user_data: auth_schema.UserSignUpData,
    session: AsyncSession,
):
    result = await session.execute(
        select(UserDB).where(UserDB.email == user_data.email)
    )
    if result.scalar_one_or_none():
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Email already registered")

    result = await session.execute(
        select(UserDB).where(UserDB.email == user_data.email)
    )
    if result.scalar_one_or_none():
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Username already used")

    hashed_password = get_password_hash(user_data.password)
    new_user = UserDB(
        email=user_data.email,
        password=hashed_password,
        username=user_data.email,
    )

    session.add(new_user)
    await session.commit()
    await session.refresh(new_user)
    return new_user


async def signup_user(
    data: auth_schema.UserSignUpData,
    session: AsyncSession,
):
    return await create_user(data, session)

The Makefile

Outside the core backend Python concerns, I have come to appreciate making use of tools like make to simplify invocation of common command line tools — like starting a FastAPI server, starting a pytest session, and so on.

# Makefile

run-local:
	fastapi dev app/main.py

test-local:
	pytest -s --cov

coverage-report:
	coverage report

coverage-html:
	coverage report && coverage html

In order to use the make tool you have to have make installed on your computer.

With this file in place at the root of my project, whenever I want to start my FastAPI server, I can do so with the following command:

make run-local

Instead of typing out the full command. This contributes to increased productivity when running certain command line tools over and over again.

Conclusion

I ignored setup for database connections in this template.

Maintaining a modular project structure and codebase does more for you down the line than you might think. A predictable and reasonable organization of functionality and tools gives beauty to a codebase beyond the functionality itself.

Inasmuch as this pattern has improved my productivity in the past year, I actively seek to learn and adopt better and better approaches to constructing and crafting my backend infrastructure.
